title: Eye Tracking in Science Education Research: Comprehensive Literature Review
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the growing use of eye-tracking (ET) technology in science education research and asks what trends, methods, and topics characterize the literature. The authors aim to synthesize how ET has been used to reveal learners’ visual attention, cognitive processing, and engagement with scientific materials and tasks, and to identify methodological patterns and research gaps across the field.

The paper is a systematic literature review of 170 empirical ET studies published in Web of Science-indexed journals and conference papers. The review examined publication trends, countries and regions represented, school levels, science subjects, sample sizes, ET hardware and software, metrics, research designs, performance measures, and additional methods such as tests, think-aloud protocols, and interviews. Most studies were conducted in Europe and mainly involved university students, though some included lower-secondary, upper-secondary, elementary, and preschool learners; a small number involved teachers or compared students with teachers.

The review concludes that ET has been especially used to study reading of learning materials, scientific representations, problem-solving, experiments/simulations, and video-based learning. Common findings suggest that expertise, prior knowledge, and spatial ability strongly shape visual processing, while instructional supports such as cues, gaze replays, and other interventions can improve comprehension and performance. The authors also highlight methodological limitations in the literature, including small samples, inconsistent reporting of hardware/software and calibration details, and underexplored areas such as emotional responses and self-regulation. They call for broader populations, stronger methodological consistency, and more meta-analytic work.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic literature review, but it is not a meta-analysis and does not synthesize a pooled causal effect estimate. The evidence base it summarizes is largely observational, mixed-method, and methodologically heterogeneous, with many small studies.
impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests instructional interventions and eye-tracking-informed design can improve science comprehension and performance, but the paper does not provide a generalizable effect size or a single intervention result. The impact is therefore plausible but unclear in magnitude at the broad K-12 level.

finding.finding_summary: This systematic review of 170 eye-tracking studies in science education reports that instructional interventions can enhance learners' comprehension and performance significantly, especially when visual cues, integration instructions, or eye-movement modelling are used. Across the reviewed literature, eye-tracking metrics such as fixation duration, dwell time, and transitions were used to examine scientific reasoning and problem-solving with scientific representations, though the paper does not report a single pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Comprehension, performance on science tasks, and eye-movement metrics during reading/problem-solving with scientific representations
finding.study_size: n=170 studies reviewed; median sample size=36 participants per study
